div1.head: Interview with Charles Jones, Mary Ellen Jones [October 10, 2001]

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: I enlisted on January 15, 1942, approximately six -- five, six weeks after Pearl Harbor, purely for the simple reason that they told me I would not be deferred. I had two years of college completed. They wouldn't defer me to finish the time in college and then go in immediately, so, in other words, I went to the Federal Building, right on Public Square, downtown Cleveland, in the basement, enlisted in the ground crew of the United States Army Air Force at that time, which is since now the United States Air Force since 1947, and went, first of all, to Fort Benjamin Harrison, outside of Indianapolis, Indiana. I was there maybe one, two weeks, and then they sent me up to Selfridge Field, which is in Mt. Clemens, Michigan, about 30 miles from -- east of Detroit. And a unique situation in my case was, when I was put into the 2nd Fighter Squadron of the 52nd Fighter Group, I was with that unit from that day -- day one -- until I was discharged in Fort Dix in late June of 1945, which not too many people in the military tell me that they never had that experience of staying with the same group of fellas, working on the same kind of airplanes for three, three-and-half years' time, and never get separated. The only way you got separated was something happened, you wasn't there anymore. That could happen in different ways.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What planes did you work on?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: We started out in the United States before we went overseas. We had what they called the Airacobra, the Bell Airacobras, made in Pennsylvania -- I think it was Buffalo -- it was a nose wheel on that fighter plane, a vee-12 inline engine. It had a cannon going right through the hub of the propeller, so that it had a larger wallop than the machine guns in the wing, but the only problem is that made it that the engine had to be behind the pilot's seat, and that didn't work out well when the plane crashed, because, when the plane crashed, you had a great big heavy 12-cylinder engine, in other words, coming right at you from behind, see. So most all the pilots that I talked to, that I had any connection with, said it was like -- they termed it the "flying coffin," because any kind of an accident -- see, I mean, when you stop suddenly, everything goes forward, see, so when we went overseas, we didn't see any P-39's overseas at all. We were sent -- the first group of my squadron was sent overseas in July of 1942, and we were sent over on boats. We was in a big convey which -- the convoy, I mean, which left New York Harbor, right past the Statue of Liberty, out -- up to Halifax, Nova Scotia, connected up with a group of Canadian boats that were going over, and everywhere you looked on any side, you just saw ships, and then way out you saw the naval protection boats. So, every seven minutes they changed their course, because, in those days -- it's not like today -- in those days, it took more than seven minutes for them to -- a torpedo coming from a submarine -- they had to line the ship up and all, so, get the thing in and sent out, and that took them over seven minutes, so, if you changed course, they would start lining up, and by the time they got it lined up, you've changed the direction that you went. So that, in other words, you went up to the north Atlantic, took 14 days from New York City up to the north Atlantic, after picking up those boats in Halifax, went right across and entered the -- whatever the ocean is there called -- between Ireland and England, and went up in -- Clyde River is in Scotland -- docked at Clyde, in Scotland. When we docked there, they didn't even let us off the boat, because they knew we were going to be sent to northern Ireland, which was still part of England -- it wasn't part of the free state -- because our pilots were not going to be flying P-39's or even other American planes. Our pilots were to get some training on a Spitfire -- the British Spitfire -- which we asked what the reason was -- and only being noncommissioned people, from privates up to master sergeants, we were not told. But I later found out that England had a contract with North American for the Mustangs, which had twice the gasoline capacity. The British planes could take off -- they could fly across the English Channel and go over France and get to Germany -- they would look at their gas gauges, and it's half gone, so they had to turn around and go back, or bail out partway back, because they would run out of gas. So, they were buying the first Spit-- the first Mustang planes from the United States before the American pilots were even going to be able to fly their own planes, you know. So, we were there maybe, you know three weeks or a month in Ireland. They said that's the farthest we can get you away from the European continent is to put you in northern Ireland. We were there near Belfast and Londonderry, where there is one or two airfields there that they would go out -- the pilots would go out and fly those planes -- and they were totally different than the P-39. They had the engine in front just like the Mustang does, but they were smaller, lighter planes, so they maneuvered better, but they didn't have the gasoline capacity, and they didn't have the fire power that the American Mustang plane did, see. So, after we got trained for that, we were sent back to Clyde again, when they decided that they were going to open the front in north Africa, which was November of 1942, about at the end of the first week, I imagine. Why, we were sent on British ships; some left from Clyde, where we were; some left from South Hampton, in England. Anyhow, to get three places that they were going in at: Casablanca; we landed at -- the Central Task Force was Oran, in Algeria; and others were landing or coming in in the third place, called Algiers, Algeria. There was three different landing spots where the opening of the European -- from the European side -- the southern side, I better call it -- of the Mediterranean, and we had -- they kept us on the boat two days extra after we had docked. We said, "What are we still sitting here for?" Well, they had to wait 'til the infantry captured airfields to fly our planes from, and having the Spitfires with not enough gasoline capacity for sufficiency in combat, the Spitfires had to fly from England, land at Gibraltar, which was under control of Great Britain, gas up in there, then come over and fly across a short space across the Mediterranean and land either at our locations south of Oran, in Algeria. And we started out two days after the landings on an air base in north Africa, started working our way towards Tunisia. And every move from then on was with these old-styled DC-3's that used to be the commercial planes here in the early part, you know; they would be two twin-engines put out by Douglas. They were very sturdy and capable planes. They had torn the insides out and made them cargo; even enlarged the door to make them cargo. And all of our equipment was -- every time you moved, you had a box for everything, and you had the weight -- including the weight of the box -- so that the pilots -- there is two pilots -- and maybe half a dozen of us guys and then the cargo in each plane. And they'd -- we would jump from one place to another -- we wouldn't be in the air -- when you moved with a plane like that -- you wouldn't be in the air more than half an hour, forty-five minutes, and you have gone a hundred miles, so you would be coming down and landing at another base that you will be for another month or so, see, and worked our way all the way across finally. The first places that we got sent to, our place, when we had the most chance of danger, we were a forward echelon landing in Bone, which still was in Algeria, but right near the orderline of Tunisia, and so when we was that close, the German planes -- in other words -- were stationed in places in Tunisia yet, 'cause Rommel hadn't got chased back that far yet to be out of Africa yet, and -- so the German air bases would have Messerschmitt 109's, and Stuka bombers, and stuff like that. They would leave from their bases, coming not to get the people, but to destroy equipment, you know, any planes on the ground, any kind of anti-aircraft for our -- for protecting our own -- tried to destroy that. Of course, some personnel, if they didn't get out of the way, were killed just by accident, but they were after damaging the equipment, so that it wouldn't be there to fight against them. And that was their idea -- procedure -- for doing it. So, my statement for the whole time we were in North Africa, we finally worked over -- our last location in North Africa, after Rommel had started up Italy, why, was Tunis -- the town, Tunis -- in Tunisia, see. And we had an airbase there for a while, while Rommel was in the southermost part, see, of Italy. And so, as they started driving them up , we were moved by these DC-3's, put our stuff in boxes, and moved to another place. The next stop, we stopped just -- a town called Monreal, outside of Palermo, in Sicily, and then we went -- after being there maybe not more than a month -- over to Corsica, another island -- that's the island where Napoleon was born. Ajaccio. I went and saw that museum there, you know, on a 24-hour pass, when I could leave -- had the chance to leave the air base, and somebody else did your work for that day, you know (laughing) and went up to see -- to me, he was another guy -- found out in World War II, there's another nutty guy like Hitler, you know. He knew a lot, but, in other words, everybody depended upon him calling the shots, like Hitler did the same, see. And there's no question in my mind that we discussed that the Americans had all the darkness time for whatever you wanted to do, because the British were doing the night work, and the American Air Force was doing the daytime work. So, we could not understand some of the things. And, as I say, low down in rank, nobody told you, it was all surely guessing, see, that we did not understand why are we moving from here to here. But the first sergeant says, "It isn't for you to know the reason why, but it's for you to do or die." And, so, we just went and done our jobs (laughs). So, finally, when we left Corsica, being a month there at the most, and sent out missions towards Italy, see -- Corsica sits between that part of France and Spain that ducks down there, and then the part of Italy, and so, therefore, we left and moved to a town in southern Italy: Fano, F-A-N-O, if that's the right pronunciation. We were there for awhile, because the bombers at that time were still coming from north Africa with all kinds -- big tanks and those four-engine bombers, like the B-24's and the B-17's. They would take off from right along the coast of North Africa, come across the narrow section there of the Mediterranean to the bottom of Italy. As soon as they would come over that northern part, then our planes would take off and take them as far to the targets as they saw they could do, and, naturally, we were always 25, 30 miles from what I called "no man's land," because our planes, even though they had more gasoline capacity than the Spitfire did, you still had less gasoline capacity than the bombers did. So you wanted to pick them up just before they started getting to unfriendly territory, see, and take them in as far to the target, like even the bomber pilots said -- and the fighter pilots, too -- as soon as they took them to the target and the bombers let go of their bombs, it was every plane for himself, head back to your base, you know, and turn and get out of there. So, like I say, we finally kept going further up. The next town we moved up to was called Foggia, right about halfway up the Adriatic coast -- it's the one between Italy and over to -- I don't know what it would be -- on the other side -- like Romania, or, you know, in the direction towards Greece, see. But, anyhow, we were on -- not the side where Naples and that area -- and so we were at Foggia for awhile, see, another month or --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have the Mustangs at that point?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: We got the Mustangs -- once we left North Africa -- we had like, the first year, I would say, a good first year or 12, 13, 14 months -- Spitfires -- and once Great Britain says, yes, now this is as many as we want, then we started to get them. The first ones we got, because, I suppose, of the speed or progression of the war, were the P-51B's, they were called, and they looked just like a Messerschmitt 109, because they had -- the canopy had these braces between these different sections of plexiglass, which caused, as the pilots say, blind spots, see, so we got those kind painted olive drab. After those either wore out, or were shot down, or something, we started getting them coming just plain aluminum color with the American star on the side, you know, the white star in the blue circle. They were never painted -- they just "get them over there, get them over there," you know. And so, like I said, then they came with the teardrop canopy, which had no braces, except where it connected at the front and touched the fuselage at the rear of it; and the pilot could look around -- well, the wing was in the way that he couldn't see directly down. That was one situation that I remembered from north Africa, when we were being attacked, you know, at least once or twice a week, if not often -- oftener (sic). The German pilots at that time in those small planes were very experienced pilots, and what they would come to do when they would come to strafe your equipment, they wouldn't fly it rightside up, they went like this. They had, in other words, fuel injectors at that time, in 1942, which even our P-51's still had the carburators on it, and when you turned that upside down, the float drops out in the carburetor, and for a moment or a few seconds seconds, until you get back over this way again so gravity would put that back in place, you know, your engine -- you could hear the cut in the engine, you know. So, in other words, we fought the whole war, you know, ended up south of Florence -- Florenzia there, it looks like -- but the English pronounciation is Florence -- in kind of the northern half of Italy, when in May, in early May, about the 5th, 7th of May, when the military in Germany decided to surrender, see, so that's the pattern we did all the way through.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, were you responsible for one particular airplane?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: One plane. I happened to be -- until we got into northern Italy -- I happened to be an assistant crew chief on the Spitfire, and I was with a fella, Elmer Dalegrove, who was from Greenbay, Wisconsin. He had gone to Schnook Field, in Rantoul, Illinois, and got American type planes -- he was called a crew chief for the inline engines, you know, the ones that have to have coolant-- see, the radial engines was in the P-47's, but a radial engine wasn't in the Spitfire. It was the same kind of an engine. And, on that basis, in other words, one way an inline engine plane can be damaged is if a shell goes through the engine, and it will drain out all of the antifreeze, see, and it just freezes. (His wife interjects, and they are talking about the cars in the driveway.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, were you in Foggia the whole time, until the end of the war, then, or --

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: No, I said we moved from Foggia -- the last place we were, Florence --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Florence?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: South of Florence, because that's further north, see. We kept closing up, so, for the fighter planes, we was closer to the no-man -- you kept moving up, so that the fighter planes would have more distance to fly from their air base, because they are closer to the target.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Could they fly to Germany from that point?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Yes, they could, because we put two belly tanks, as they called them -- when there was a long mission, there was 75 gallons of gas over in this -- it looked like a little balloon or something, you know, at most maybe shaped like a football -- and 75 gallons here and 75 gallons here, and what the pilots could do -- they had on the instrument panel -- they could switch and take some gas out of this, and then turn that out of this. To keep the weight, see, even, they would switch from tank to tank; and as soon as they would use all the gas out of both engines, just dropped them like a bomb. You saw more belly tanks going through Italy and on up there and in that direction than you could shake a stick at. I thought how many we went through, and there were a lot from the other air bases, you know, dropping belly tanks, and somebody someplace sees this lightweight aluminum tank, _______+ were right in the middle of it, it was round at the bottom and top, and bigger at the back and tapered back. Like I say, there's a lot of belly tanks over there after the war was over, you know, what somebody hadn't crocked, you know, and wanted to use it for some of their own personal purposes, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get pretty close to any of your pilots?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Oh, yes. Like I say, I got the names of all of them. My pilot -- I was assistant crew chief -- and, like I say, Elmer Dalegrove, from Greenbay, was the head crew chief. And we had -- our names was on the plane just like the pilot's name; and his name was James S. Varnell. He was from Tennessese. His middle name was Sullivan, and he liked to be called -- he wanted us -- Lieutenant, and then Captain and Major -- he wanted to be called "Sully." He says, "We are in this together." He was from Tennessee. He says, "We aren't worried about rank." He says, "We are just here for the war." "But," he says, "if you see some of the generals or the bigshots around," he said, "you better call us by the name." But he says, "You are taking care of our planes"; and he said, "We have got to be a team," see. So, I think, my own judgment from what we did, whether he was going on a mission that day or not, you started up each plane every day. I'm about 5-foot-6 -- lock the brakes, you know, put chalks under the wheels, run it up to full throttle, and then you could check the mags, 24 spark plugs, you know, intake and exhaust spark plug, because it was a 12-cyclinder engine, and that would show you whether you had a bad spark plug, see. You would switch it, and, boy, the plane was out on the ground bouncing like that (making a shaking sound), so then you would have to check out and find which plug it was, and take that out. So, if that happened, you checked that that morning, and the mission was going to be close after you checked it for leaving, that plane stayed on the ground, and you put in one of these other planes, like I say, one of the P-51B's, which had the disadvantages, but at least it was working when the other one had a problem, see; and you didn't let it go off, see, without that. So, to me, like I say, we were fortunate. He shot down 17 German planes of different kinds, you know. Sometimes they were a cargo plane carrying something, and other times it would be a German bomber. Another time it would be in a dogfight with another fighter plane, shoot it down, see. He had 17 credits for himself, Sully Varnell, from Tennessee. And you couldn't have found -- of course, there was no integration at that time. We had -- the next airfield to us in Italy, solid black fellas: black ground crew, black, you know, pilots, like that -- and then maybe a mile, mile-and-a-half down the road, one way or the other, and they would be taking off from their airfield, and we would be taking off from ours, and be going with whichever set of bombers they were told to go with, you know. And so, like I say, you got really close with the fellas, I mean, we knew that, you know. \tab Like I said, here I am on the ground, the first thing we did at any place when we moved to is dug foxholes. In other words, that was our first -- don't pitch your tents, don't do that, that's not as important as having this place to go. And, of course, like I said, in north Africa we did the same thing, so that when we were getting bombed and strafed, there was schrapnel, you know, when a bomb was dropped, all this heavy metal, you know, like arrows shooting in all directions, you better be down under ground level. Like I said, I didn't have to dig the foxholes very deep, you know. I didn't have to dig down very far, because I'm only 5'6" already, you know. So, like I say, when all the planes would take off, the first sergeant would say to you, "Well, if you had been smart at all, you would get out of the way." So, you didn't have to tell me twice, you know. I may not have been very big, but I could run fast, so getting into the foxhole -- well, that's another thing from the British, they allowed us to use their radar. So, when these German planes would be taking off in Tunis, there, coming when we were still in Algeria yet -- like this town of Bone, or even further west than that -- why, as soon as they got 500 feet above the ground, the radar could pick them up. Well, we had ten minutes then -- with a plane like that -- see, in those days, maybe like our P-51, 350, 375, where it would be pretty close to top speed, see -- and you had 10 minutes to get your planes in the air, and then get out of the way, see. And like I say, they bombed -- they, the Germans -- bombed and strafed the fields in north Africa, but once we got into Sicily and Corsica and started up Italy, it appeared to me, having been a coach in my school teaching career, I would say the Germans were then on the defense, not the offense. In other words, they were just kind of backing off and trying to hold what they had, apparently, and they were not wasting their time and maybe some personnel and, you know, equipment, too. So, for the first year or 14 months, whatever it was in north Africa, from then on, like I say, as long as I was smart enough to get into the foxhole, you know -- and I didn't even have to do that very much once we started in Italy. We had some scares in Corsica, because the northern part of Corsica is not too far from the French coast, down there where I think Lyons or some of those towns are, down in the southern part, that have -- one of them, I think, has a gambling place at now, you know -- I don't know if it was there during World War II -- but I mean it is there now. Like I say, it was a whole different war from my standpoint, once we left Italy, because you did your work to keep crowding the Germans back to their own territory. And, as I said, the difference between Napoleon and Hitler, you know, they wanted to run the whole show. Like the same thing -- I had no part of it, except our pilots were involved in June '44, when they were going to land in Normandy, and those places there. On my discharge, it shows our pilots were covering for what it said southern France and northern France, see, because when we were far enough up in Italy there, you could just go across there with the bombers that were trying to bother the Germans, you know, and the pilots could go with them, because we were up there near Florence, in Italy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any particularly bad air raids when you were in Africa?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Well, I don't know if you would call them bad. I would say, not really. Most of our persons that got hurt in the war, they called it "in the line of duty," meaning, like, if they would find a German motorcycle, let's say, because this was one of the accidents. It had a side car -- I don't know if you have ever watched Hogan's Heroes that used to be on TV, you know, with Colonel Klink and all those guys -- a lot of that was accurate, as far as I was concerned. They, you know, tinkered -- because they were aircraft mechanics -- they tinkered around and got the motorcycle running, and it had the side car on it. And, gee, they were going down the road, and what the Germans had done -- in other words -- they put a post on this side and a post on this side, and a wire across, see, and a motocycle -- they didn't have any shields -- they were decapitated, see. We lost two or three guys like that. One guy was driving a jeep, but instead of having the windhield up, it was laying on the hood, and so the wire was able to get the guy driving the jeep, you know. So, those who were sent home, in the instructions, they were killed in the line of duty. Well, I mean, they stretched a point, I guess, maybe to what I would say is. I spent probably as much time doing guard duty as I did being an assistant mechnic on an airplane, because they would ship us 100 or 100-plus octane gasoline in 55-gallon drums; and when you got them brought to you with the trucks in 55-gallon drums, you -- you wanted -- well, they stacked them three high -- five-foot six -- the third one, I can't see over the top, see. So, when I -- you were supposed to walk your post in a military manner, go this way for a while and that way for a while -- in other words, I did a lot of guard duty overseas, because, as an assistant crew chief, you could just say to the crew chief, well, for four hours while your assistant is -- you had a four-hour shift -- while he is on guard duty -- why, in other words, d\qc 14 d you'll function by yourself, and when he comes back, he will help you again. And they tried to -- I kind of thought at times, you know, gee, it seems like I am getting an awful lot of guard duty, you know. Somebody else -- maybe they knew somebody, and they didn't get guard duty, you know. But, that could have -- I figured I was sitting on a keg of dynamite. If one drum goes, the whole bunch of them goes (laughing), stacked three high, you know, 55-gallons of high-octane gas in one tank (laughing), you know. They had trucks, you know, where they pumped the gasoline out of that into -- just like they deliver to gas stations, at the gas stations here -- and they would come to the planes, like you see at the airport, you know. And, of course, it didn't take as long to fill up a fighter plane with gasoline as it does these planes like they used on September 11th, those, you know, 757's or 767's. Gasoline -- and they claim they had only left from Boston, and to get down to New York, they couldn't have used a heck of a lot of gas, even though they have got four engines, if you have them full, so it may not have been called a bomb, but that was a bomb when it exploded. Each one hit a different building there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did Sullie make it out okay?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Tell you the story about our pilot, Sullie. He got up very close to 50 missions. He had holes and stuff in his plane, but never shot down. He came back, and they said, okay, you want to go back, take 30 days back in the states for R&R -- as they called it -- rest and relaxation, and stuff. So, he was back in the United States. So, while he was back for his 30 days -- I don't know who did it -- but the story given to us that were maintaining the planes like for him and other pilots that were doing the same thing, they said would he help train -- they were starting to train some of our young kids, 18 and 19-year-old kids on these fighter planes, and the Americans still, in '45, were using propellor planes, not jet planes. The Germans were flying some jet fighters around, we saw; but, in other words, they didn't have that many of them. And they asked him if he would help train them. He said when they take off for a flight for a mission, they go -- they have the head guy, you know, and then the two wingmen. Well, four-bladed props, and they were just outside of Baltimore, Maryland, going down the runway -- he up front -- and the one guy lost control of his plane. Anyway, the propellor went through his cockpit, and he got killed on the spot. And we said, "Gee, that doesn't seem fair," and the guy says, "Well, who said life is fair?", and I said, yeah, but here the guy shot down 17 planes, and he is helping out to train younger guys, because the war wasn't over yet, and that was about in April, and the war -- Germans didn't stay until about the first week in May -- and he gets killed in April, you know, on a practice thing to help train a few more younger ones, and with the propellor. Now, I think if the plane -- if that had been a jet -- those jets like they have got now, fighter planes, see, there is no rotating prop that's out where it could have gone into there, and he would have had a chance; but, see, the propellor went right through -- that one guy's plane went right into the cockpit of his plane, so he didn't even last until the last day of the war in Europe, and here he got it here at home. A sad thing, you know. We all felt bad, but you can't change what's -- you know, what happens. So, like I say, I came home, and I got the same points for, you know, whatever battles or whatever missions they went on, and so forth, I got the same points. You had to have 85 to be discharged. I had 115, because Sullie Varnell had 115. The other pilots in our squadron had 115, 'cause they all went on the same missions, you know. Get back the first day, we landed -- Patrick Henry was a base there in Virginia someplace, and we were there maybe a week or two weeks, and this was in June of '45. The war with Japan wasn't over yet, but -- and then they sent me from there to Fort Dix for discharge, because, in other words, discharges were based on the number of points you had. So, they had three or four lines: ones that wanted total discharge, ones that wanted ROTC, or ones that just wanted to re-enlist. Well, you can imagine which line was the longest line by far -- those who wanted immediately out (laughing), including myself, you know. I had finished two years of college, and they wouldn't defer me, so I wanted to get back and finish -- to get four years of college in. And, so, like I say, I had 115, and I got in that longest line, which took a long time to get through it, but I was willing to wait out the length of the line, you know, and I got discharged. I was back home by the 26th of June, in 1945. At that time, the Pennsylvania Railroad cut across Euclid Avenue, about 55th Street, in Cleveland. I got on from Fort Dix, went to Philadelphia, and then there is the Pennsylvania Railroad there, take that. I got off there at 55th Street and came down off the railroad, went right across, you know, overhead there, and my dad and mother were waiting where the people could stand at the street level down there, and put me in the car and went to where they were living at that time, in Cleveland, see. So, I mean, I am sort of doing a lot of generalizations, but I do appreciate the fact that Uncle Sam paid for my third and fourth years of college, and for the books. Of course, I had to pay my own room and board like either at a dormitory, which I took the cheaper way; I found a house in Kent. I tried to get into Ohio State, and they said that we have got too many down here already, you know, at that time when I got out at the end of June. They said, "We are packed for September already," see. So, okay, I contacted Kent State, and they said, "We are packed for September, but we can take you if you want to start in January '46." I said, "That's good to me," because Ohio State didn't say any time they thought that I could go. So, I had to go -- I dropped -- lost three-quarter hours of credit at Finn College, because I had started out in engineering. My dad wanted me to do that out of high school, and after the time in the service and the time before I could get into college, I had lost four years. I didn't want to have to go back and audit a class or, you know, take it for a second time for credit, because that means it's not getting me any further ahead. So, I said I did well in math in high school, and the math classes that I took at college in the two years of credit I had. So, I said I will just go and take -- go into education and teach math, because -- in other words, my math teacher at Orange School, when I was going there, interested me in math, and I said I will try to see if I can interest kids in math like he got me interested in math. I mean, the only thing I was an A student in, in school, was in math, but I could get B's in stuff, like history; and my worst area in college was English. They wanted a theme for a thesis, any thesis, or this or that, terrible. In other words, even when I started at Kent, after the war, for the education degree down at Kent, to be a teacher, you had to take some English or literature classes, you know, freshmen college level, and I know darn well I was getting C's in high school, that I wouldn't even be doing that well in college, because there is some elimination or some don't go to college, see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Speaking of writing, do you remember much about getting letters when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Yeah. Oh -- at that time, I got from my parents and like that, but not very much. I wrote to a couple of girls that was in my graduating class from Orange School, and they would write back maybe once or twice in a year's time. So, both of those that wrote to me, when I got home, why, once I got a car, I went and visited them. In fact, the one girl is still single, today, that attends our class reunions. We should have another one in 2002, but when you have been out of high school 65 years in 2002, I don't think there are going to be too many around, or if they are around, they are not mobile enough to get there, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a lot of packages and things like that?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Oh, well, I got that saxophone sent to me, like I said.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's true. I don't think we put that on tape.

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Oh, we didn't?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Yeah. Well, just to repeat it briefly again. My father was working at Clark Control, across the street from the General Electric Lamp place on East 105th Street, in Cleveland, near Collinwood High School. He knew some of the fellas in the shop there. He said, "Here's the saxophone case," you know, "Make a protective covering around it." And he sent my alto sax across from Cleveland, Ohio, there, you know, sent it across, and it came to me -- I am not sure which town I was in at the time, but it was one of these towns when I was in north Africa. And, like I say, I have a picture here, I took the picture, I wasn't in the picture myself -- that was our little picture of our little -- some of the time we would have seven, some of the time we would have eight. Never a piano player, because that's too hard of work to get around. Like I say, I am not in that picture, but the other guys that I played with are in the picture.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you play a lot then?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Well, I wouldn't call it a lot. I would say, like, mostly when we were in north Africa. I don't remember doing it at all in Italy, because once we were squeezing them in, there was the danger of more chances that they got shorter distance to get to you, see. But, like I say, they didn't seem to be trying that. So, I would say, we played, maybe for sure, it averaged once a month. And the USO, in New York City, would send us all the orchestrations for any instrument you wanted, or they will send you the whole thing, and if you don't want them, why, just keep 'em and file 'em in the circular file, or something. They sent me the alto sax. And the other fella -- Bob Jenner is in that picture; he played the tenor sax. He lived in New York state. Like I say, they would send you whatever you wanted. Another fella, like I say, played the trumpet. Another black guy played the guitar, and things like that, so we always had anywheres (sic) from six to eight people, and we had the up-to-date -- like they play on this channel WRMR, you know, all of that kind of music. And, like I say, it was always close enough to where Red Cross would bring to the airfield, even in North Africa, it would -- doughnuts and coffee, before they would leave for the mission. And that didn't always go so well with enlisted guys like myself, but I didn't make that much out of it. This one friend of mine that lived in Detroit, Michigan, Donald Lowell, he said he didn't understand it; and I said, "Understand what?" They said the doughnuts and coffee are for the pilots, and if there is any left, the enlisted men can have it, see. So, he says, "Aren't we fightin' the same war that they are?" And I says, "Well, I don't really care for coffee anyhow." And I said, "So what if I don't get a doughnut?"; I said, "I won't blimp up or something," you know. But he was really put out. \tab Jones, my grandfather Jones -- my father's father -- came over to this country from Wales as a bachelor, a 40-year-old bachelor, in 1885. They hadn't even opened Ellis Island yet. That didn't open until about 1890 or '92. He was docked at Boston. He met my grandmother at Boston, and that's where the Jones family started from. 1885 is when he got to this country. \tab My wife, her maiden name is Macy -- M-A-C-Y -- like the store in New York City. Well, there were two Macy brothers. It was the other Macy brother, John, I think it was, that started that store, and his brother is the start of my wife's line. So, she can trace -- her sister did it, actually -- trace it back to 1657, when the first Macy left England -- they were English -- and came to this country, and most of them landed on some big island off the coast of Boston or Nantucket, or something, off of the coast of Boston. They mainly landed there and eventually got onto the basic part of Massachusetts there, see. So, like I say --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You talk about the USO. Did you ever get any shows?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Oh, well, I can remember two (door opening). But anyhow, like I say, Frances Langford and Bob Hope were there to perform for us when we were in Palermo, Sicily. These "Four Joes and a Jeep" was in north Africa, and there was one other one. But there wasn't anybody that I recognized the name, you know, before I left the states, see. But, when they said "Bob Hope," and I said, "Oh, we have got to go see Bob Hope and Frances Langford," _____+, and the young fella playing the guitar, you know, would kind of be the accompaniment for her when she did this --

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: And then he fired them at you one right after another, so I would be remembering (laughing) on TV, before his health got so bad; like he is hanging in there yet, but I don't think he is enjoying life the way he is right now. But, see, he is another guy that -- SWOPE: He is ninety-eight now.

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Yeah. As I say, he came -- his name is on that one bridge there. His father was the engineer -- that Carnegie Bridge there, in Cleveland, that's his father. Some people think when they call it the Hope Memorial Bridge, they think of the Bob Hope (laughing); it is his father, you know. He brought the family over, you know, to this country, and I think Bob was not in school yet, maybe four-, five-, six-years-old, something like that. So, he did his whole childood, you know, in the United States, living basically in the greater Cleveland area, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does one vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: The only vivid memory is the times when -- in north Africa, you know -- when you had to really -- when the Germans were active -- that you had to really -- if you didn't get underground, get below ground level. But I would have to say, honestly, after north Africa, I didn't feel I -- the place I thought I was in most danger was guarding a gasoline dump, and nothing happened. And to this day, whenever they see me -- we had our 12th reunion, the 13th to the 16th of September, out in Albany, Illinois. The mess sergeant was the staff sergeant that fed us our meals three times a day; he accepted the challenge of, you know, making the arrangements for us to come in there, and where's motels and what do we see while we are there, and had to have time left for our business meeting. And, like I say, I only felt in danger, you know, either in north Africa, because of the Germans, and not knowing what danger might be -- I had a gun. My father wouldn't let us have a gun. We didn't have a gun in the house, just my sister and I, and my mother and father during the whole Depression, all the 30's. We didn't have a gun anyplace near, because somebody'll -- they won't take the shell out, or something, and somebody pulls the trigger, and somebody is hurt or killed, you know. \tab So, I goes into the service, you know. I decided I am going to enlist, because I said I wasn't valedictorian in my class at Orange School. I was maybe in the top ten, but not -- nowheres (sic) near the top, and I said but I would like to, you know, make it through, if I go in. And I'm 22-years-old and Pearl Harbor occurred, and they told me you can't get deferred, that I was in the same -- the Draft Board, Shaker Heights City Hall, on the corner of Van Aken and Lee Road. It is still there today, second floor office.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any specific memories of the day Pearl Harbor was bombed?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Sure. That was a Sunday. I remember -- we had a radio in our home. We had just got home from Sunday School and church, and I just flipped on, you know, to see if there is a ball game, you know, baseball. Cleveland baseball team was lousy back then, like it has been a lot of the times in the past, see. And I flipped on the switch, and, you know, they cut in, you know, and they said Pearl Harbor has been bombed by the Japanese, you know. So, I remember that as plain as day. We had just got in the house, took our hats and coats off, you know. It was in December, see, and we had coats and hats on, and we were going in the car to church, and that, and so, flipped that on. I said, gee, you know. Like I said, I was 22 in September, and here's Pearl Harbor happens two or three months after that, see. So, I had already, you know -- 1940 -- October 1940, was when they started the peacetime draft. I had to go in and sign up then. So, I know I had a number, see, for when they did the drawings; they would draw numbers. And I hadn't been called, you know, up to that point, and they started that October 1940. Some had been called in even when we weren't in the war with anybody yet, and so I figured, you know, now we were surely in the war, what do I do now? Well, I got two years -- well, actually it was three years, because at Finn College, which is Cleveland State -- Cleveland State now, but was Finn College -- you had what they called the co-op plan. You had to do the freshman year -- the complete freshmen year, three quarters for the freshmen year; then, after that, whatever amount of time, quarters that you stayed in college, they would find you a job following that term to get -- earn some money to come back for some more quarters, see. They called it a co-op plan. So, I was in that. So, I had used up three years, but one of the years was time that I was on the job, which I got money for books when I came back, and that, but that didn't give me any good quarters credit towards graduation, see. So, that only totaled two years of credit. So, when I came back, I decided I can't go back into engineering, because I said at Orange School, I only had three years of math in high school, because it was such a small school. They only had one high school math teacher who taught math, starting with the ninth grade level on up, and he would have more than two or three sections of the same class. You know, they had smaller classes. Being a school teacher myself, I know there was much more advantage if you are teaching in a smaller class, because then you can help more kids, see. When I had smaller classes, I could get -- show the kids -- demonstrate what to do, and they could start on it. So, okay, we have this last ten minutes to get started on the assignment, then I could go up and down the aisle, and here's a kid sitting there, and he is not ready to start at all, 'cause he don't know where to start from first base. But if you get 25 kids in a class, your hands are full. And, today, with the removal of discipline in schools, because you can't do this and you can't do that, in other words, that's, you know -- that's a losing cause, because some kids are not in school to learn, they are in school to play around and cause trouble, you know, and what they are doing is hurting other kids that want to learn, see. So, like I say, I got my 30 years in. I didn't start teaching until I was 28-years-old. I started the first day of teaching -- I was 28-years-old on September 1st -- we started teaching the day after Labor Day -- and that was Labor Day -- the 2nd of September, 1947. \tab You came down 306. Did you go through Chester?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: You must have passed the three-story building? That's the school, there, that's got the windows broken out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: See -- the first job.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was your first job?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: In that building there, on the third floor in that building, you know. See, that one-floor part on the one side, that's been built in recent years, maybe 20, 30 years ago, but I started teaching there in September of 1947, up on the third floor. You can see that it goes on the side; it has got three levels to the older building, see. I was teaching math there, you know. Two other new teachers there, and I will never forget that situation myself. I started teaching, 28-years-old, see. They are just out of college. "Oh, Mr. Jones," they said, "You look a little older than we are." "Yes," I said, "about maybe six years or maybe more." And they said, you know, like, "What happened to you, did you flunk or something," you know (laughing). I says, "Oh," I said, "I had to go back and finish two more years of college after I got out of World War II, before I would even have enough to have a bachelor's degree," see. So I finished -- I could go full-time, you know, when I came out. I went summer term and everything, started January 1946, graduated in August, which meant I went to summer school, the summer before and then the second summer, and got enough quarters in and credits in, so that I finished the last week in August, and I wasn't -- I hadn't gotten my diploma from college. I got my job lined up, 'cause I told them I am coming up, and the superintendant up there hired me to start the first day of school, September 2nd, and I think I got my diploma about the 20th or the 21st of August (laughing), you know. That was my experience, so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That covers your veteran's experiences pretty good, though, then?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Oh, like I say, there is a lot more incidental stuff, you know, different things that happened, you know, between different ones. Just a little one in passing, you know. It's hard to believe, there was another guy and I went on a 24-hour pass when we was in north Africa, see. And there would be a lot of places where it was big, open fields, you know. Gee, I mean, a long distance before anything or an obstacle, you know. So, he and I are walking down this road, and it started getting kind of windy, and that, you know. So, I was just kind of looking around, you know. We was watching for the -- the British would pick you up in their vehicles, the same as the Americans would, and take you as far as they could in the direction you said you wanted to go. And I think I was maybe headed for -- in north Africa, I wanted to go to Carthage. There was supposed to be an antique or a real ancient civilization, or whatever you would call it. We were walking along, so I looked this way, and all of a sudden I looked back, and the guy is not standing beside me. So, I turned completely around -- and he is shorter than I. I said, "What are you doing?" He is walking behind me. He says, "Why, I thought there is no use the two of us breaking the wind." I says, "Well, when are you going to take your turn?" (laughing), see. You are shorter than me, and he says he walked beind me because I was breaking the wind for him (laughing). So, a lot of crazy things like that happened on our one or three-day pass, you know, when they could come up with something. When I was first in north Africa, in Oran, I went into -- I forget what they call those stores that you can turn something in and they will give you money for it --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Pawn shop?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Yeah, pawn. I bought a French saxophone, but when I found out how complicated they made their saxophones, that's when I told my dad send me my -- in other words, the United States saxophones had an octave key that -- you have two octaves on a saxophone, see, and when you press the octave key, if you are on the lower one, it opens the lower-down pipe. But, if you are pressing the notes up at the top of the scale, you know, it flicks it itself and opens this thing on the top where the bend of the pipe is, see, where you are blowing into. So, I got so -- so used to it taking care of itself, that I didn't have to worry about it. I would be playing that French saxophone, and it went to the next octave higher, and I had only pressed the bottom one, so -- so, I was on the wrong octave, see. I said that's too much of a pain in the -- I took it back. I told them, I said, "I forgot what I even paid you for this, but, here, sell it again, it's yours," you know, because I waited until my father sent the one over; but I went into that pawn shop in Oran, in north Africa, trying to buy a saxophone, 'cause I wanted to start this orchestra. And I said, well, I am not that good of a musician, but I said if you have got somebody playing the drum, or I can hear what the beat is, why I could stay with it better, see. (A pause)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, hey, that's very good.

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: My wife was only one year in the Army Nurse Corps, whether you wanted any information from her. See, if it hadn't been for World War II, we would have never met.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Somebody said that's fate. I said, well, I don't know what you call it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You met her when she was a nurse?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Because she grew up in Miami County, which is the county north of Montgomery, which has Dayton. Since I went with her after -- this was after World War II -- she had gone through nurses training and was a registered nurse, not a practical nurse. In those days, hopsitals trained their own people, and it was a three-year course, see. And they got actual experience on the job, you know, as part of their classwork. They would do classwork, and maybe they would have them come down for a few days and go with some of the nurses out on the floor, and see how you do this and what do you do for that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did she go overseas?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: No, no, no. That's the thing of it. If she had, we wouldn't have met, see. But, in other words, two of the three people she was closest to did get sent overseas, see. She signed up, but for some reason her name wasn't picked. So they said that's some more why it was fate, see, somebody said.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: So, she was -- Crile Hospital is where Cuyahoga Community College, in Parma, is now -- that property was an army hospital in World War II, that some people would be sent sometimes, mostly from Europe, for something very serious. You know, they would have to get them out of a field hospital and get them to where there is more equipment and everything else. So, she finished her training and everything, and they had signed up for overseas, and these other two girls, they were sent out over to the South Pacific, see. And she said, "I had my name down there, too. How come I didn't go?" They said, well they just said they wanted so many, and those were the names drawn. \tab So, where I get the laugh is the next part, see. On a Sunday morning, when my dad used to live out in Orange -- like I said, I went to Orange School. He had joined a protestant church called The Church of God church. And the one he attended was over, you know, where Euclid Beach Park Amusement Park used to be, over there on Lakeshore Boulevard -- well, East 140th is one of the streets, and then once you get to a 152nd, 156th is where Euclid Beach Park, one of the entrances was. Well, in other words, she was sent not overseas, but to that -- it was called Crile Hosptial. That was the name of one of the doctors, Dr. George Crile was one of the original doctors in the Cleveland Clinic, see. What's the Cleveland Clinic, today, gee, that covers a whole big space in downtown Cleveland there. And Crile was one of the first doctors, you know, that more or less got that going years and years ago. So they called that the Crile Hospital. \tab So, she had been there a few weeks, and then she decided -- well, she attended a church of the same denomination down near Dayton, about, you know, 15, 20 miles north of Dayton. It was in one of the small towns down there, called Troy, like we have got a Troy Township up here, but it doesn't have a post office. It's Burton post office. Down there, Troy is the county seat of Miami County, see, down there. So, she went to the Troy High School there. And in that area, like I say, there was a church of our denomination down in that area. So, she is up here and kind of lonesome, you know. Other ones are going to their churches, you know. So, at that time, the street cars, you know, had the rails right in the streets in Cleveland, you know. She took the streetcar. Well, first, I guess she had to take a bus so she could get to the streetcar that went on Pearl Road. Pearl Road is the same as Route 42, see. And it went on Pearl Road, then it went down under that one bridge, you know, in Cleveland there, to go out to the east side. At the public square, she had to transfer and get on another streetcar that was going to go down 140th Street towards Euclid Beach. She gets off and walks down the street to where the church is, you know. She comes walking in. My dad, he talked -- Mary Ellen says I do that -- but I got it partly from my dad and partly because of teaching math. I talked a lot of the time and did most of the talking in trying to get as much talking out. I said, "Ask some questions, so I know where you need help," you know. \tab So, anyhow, she comes walking in this Sunday morning. My dad was outside, and I was already seated down there, waiting for the preacher to start the church service, see. So, he just let her sit down there, but he said I want you to meet; he said this young lady says she is an army nurse out at the Crile Hospital. I said yeah, I saw the young lady come in, see. I said I recognized -- I said I saw that uniform overseas, you know, because I spent ten days for -- they called it yellow jaundice, I had when I was in the service. They said the whites of my eyes was turning yellow, and for a week or ten days all they did was give me juices, you know. Didn't give me any -- no food, just juices. So, anyhow, I said okay. So I goes out after church, and I didn't think about it, and I am waiting outside. So, my father comes walking out with her, you know, and he says I want you to meet her, you know. He says here is Mary Ellen -- her last name Macy -- like I say, from the Macy family that came from England in the early 1600's. And I said, "Well, how are you?", you know. My dad volunteers -- it was his car. He said I could drive the car, his car -- and my mother and he sat in the back seat -- and drove her, so she didn't have to take the streetcar back to Crile Hospital, out there where the ______, see, over there at the Parma campus. So, everything started from there, you know. We started dating. In other words, it was an over 200-mile trip, you know, to go down there by car, or by whatever method you went, bus, or whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your highest rank?

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: Well, it -- my highest rank was Buck Sergeant. My name was on -- on May the 1st, on the First Sergeant's tent. I was made Staff Sergeant, but the war finished on the 7th. So, I went to the Staff Sergeant, the First Sergeant of our particular enlisted unit. I said, "Hey, my name is down there." He said, "The war is over now." He says, "You won't see anything from there." My name came up, and I didn't get _______+ (laughing), so I would have to say Buck Sergeant.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Buck Sergeant.

sp.speaker: Charles Jones
sp.p: There is three up and nothing down. I would have had ______+ on the bottom side. I said, "Well," -- I said, "I think I just would rather have the war over rather than have it go longer."

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: So, my -- my impressions of the homefront would simply be we had to take our ration books with us to the trade _____ and turn in the sugar -- I guess they had sugar and meat. I was kind of -- lived in a cell that was not exposed to the world, really. We -- they had dances out at the Wright-Patterson Air Base that they would furnish transportation to the nurses who wanted to dance with the military personnel. Actually, you know -- and I wasn't involved in d\qc 31 d gas rationing, because we didn't have -- we took streetcars all over the town. None of us had any money. And the social life was pretty small, and we worked all the time. And three years, we had two weeks off in the summer, which is not very much, considering now. I would go home -- my folks lived on a farm, so we were pretty well self-contained for food. Never did -- even in the Depression -- never bought anything that wasn't necessary to the diet. So that was -- and I don't remember -- as I say, I would get rides to church with one of the members in Dayton that belonged to our church, which was fifteen miles away, I guess, or something. So, I walked -- I would go with them. And I don't know about too much, but -- for the homefront -- but I do know there were units formed from the hospital, of doctors and nurses, that went into the service, but it was, you know, we still had our own little life to live, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Specific memories of Pearl Harbor Day?

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: Yes. I was at Dayton -- I was in nurses training. It was a Sunday, of course. And I had worked that day, and in the afternoon, when -- we didn't have too many radios available either, as far as that goes. So, when I heard about it, my first thought was, I have got to go to church. It was in the afternoon. So, I did -- I don't know if I called first. But, anyhow, I went out to this family that lived in Dayton, and the young man -- it would be like a third or fourth cousin of mine -- he was a student at University of Cincinnatti, but like he was home that weekend. So, anyhow, he drove me up -- I mean the two of us went up to church that night. All I could think of was, is this the beginning of the Armegeddon? And I know when -- I guess some of my classmates knew that I was -- that I attended church on Sunday ______+. I don't know how people -- how that Aurora crew was over, but anyhow, at one of the meals shortly after that, one of them asked me, "Do you think, is this the end of the world?" They asked me. d\qc 32 d And I am, of course, 18, knowing it all. And I just -- of course I said, "I don't know." But it was a scary time. But I remember, as I say, that is what I remember about Pearl Harbor, was hearing about it, and that we were going to be at war. And that -- I thought maybe it was like the war that would end all wars, something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you have a feeling that maybe it would turn out good for us?

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: (Laughs). Actually, I don't -- I didn't even follow -- we all corresponded with people. Somebody got a list of names, and I corresponded with somebody who was in the Navy Air Force. He would fly through -- over in the Pacific area. But we didn't -- he didn't send -- we had never met. So, then the communications were like -- moron jokes were popular then. And just -- just I would say -- talk about the weather and the sunshine, you know. It was all very light and airy, not any serious stuff. I don't remember being -- we didn't have newspapers, at least I didn't follow it along. I didn't have any brothers or sisters -- brothers -- didn't have anybody -- immediate family --in the service. I did have a first cousin, who was killed in Okinawa or Guadalcanal. I don't know. He was about my age. I don't remember following the war that much, because it was just selfishly in my own little world. \tab When did I think it was going to be different? I don't know. I do know they were going to start drafting nurses in the early part of '45. And I think Frances Payne Bolton came through. She came through with the Cadet Corps Program. So, we all jumped on that bandwagon, because we were already in the training, and we could get money for it. We got thirty dollars a month, and more if we went off to another place. Some of use went up to the psychiatric hospital in Toledo. So, we were considered off-campus, so we got sixty dollars. I mean, it was -- money counts even then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the day FDR died?

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: Oh, yes. I was on duty at Crile Hospital. And -- I guess I was on duty -- and somebody -- the word came through the ward -- they had these gigantic wards there. And, of course, it was rehabiliation mostly for those -- for the servicemen that were coming back, where they did plastic surgery, replacing the face. That's the type of surgery, mostly, that was there. I remember that it was just kind of like a shock. And who is Harry Truman? Who is he? \tab Then, of course, we went -- then I remember when I was still there at Crile, when the war ended, and we were all -- nobody could go off -- what do I say -- we were kept on duty. Kept on the campus. They didn't say quarantined. What was the word they had when you -- nobody could leave?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you couldn't participate in the VE Day celebrations?

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: Oh, no, no. So, a bunch of us -- I guess all the people -- all the nurses on our floor gathered in this one room. I guess that was the day the war was officially over, maybe. And they played black poker, or something. I have never played poker in my life, but I mean we all were there sitting on the floor and playing poker. Then the next thing I did, after I heard that, was -- that the war was ended and such -- I called Bud. I said -- it was over about Labor Day, about that time. We can't -- everything was canceled. And I don't know why, but anyhow, I called him, 'cause I had only known him a couple of weeks. So, he invited me up for his family Labor Day weekend. Most disastrous day I ever thought of, because people were prim and proper. I am from a big family that everybody at once -- and here they sit and hold a cup of tea like this. And I wanted to run away. But then, of course, we had signed up for the duration, about six months, and so, in March, the list went up on the board saying those who wanted out could get out. So, I d\qc 34 d signed up to get out, and went back home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any specific memories _______+ when they announced that they had dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: No, except it's just -- I guess not really fully understanding how much damage could be done by it. I don't have any personal thoughts on it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No personal thoughts?

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: Un-uh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you think that covers most of your memories of --

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- that time?

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: My memories mostly are more school-oriented, the things I did in our training and the classmates. I mean, it was a real bonding, because we were all there under a great big umbrella, and then we would say -- some of them that would say goodbye as they were heading out for whatever service they went into.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And what was the name of the hospital you were a nurse at? What hospital most of the time during the war?

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: Just Crile, over here on the west side.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Crile.

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: Crile. We went -- our group went to Ft. Knox for basic training. Then we lost -- then most of us all came up to Crile; and from Crile, some of them went -- some of them did go to the South Pacific, about May or June of that year.

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: So, then they were over there, but then they came back and were discharged later than we were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, did you have a rank?

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: All nurses went in as 2nd Lieutenants.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 2nd Lieutenants.

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: It was automatic. And, of course, we weren't in long enough to be -- I worked with some -- some nurses that had been over in India, in the Pacific. And she talked -- she was a 1st Lieutenant, and I think she should have been a Captain, because she had been in a couple of years, and she was on a train in India, and she was telling me about -- of course, she had gotten married, too -- but, she was talking about the condition on the train ride through India, where the rats were running around, and it was very unpleasant. But I felt like a kindergarten kid in relation to her experience and knowledge. Some of them had been coming back and were reassigned to the States, I guess, for different things. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, very good. Thanks. I am especially interested in memories of Pearl Harbor, that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Mary Ellen Jones
sp.p: Well, I can't give you too much, because my memory ----

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's always a snapshot, and I have got several of these now. You know, people do have some specific little incidents or little stories about things like that, and they are all different, but everybody seems to remember it vividly. END OF SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE
